Rather than go through the rigmarole of the usual talking points about how the Left's actions have and are causing a moderate revolt against them, I'd like to just talk about what led me to not vote in this election but end up being okay with Trump winning. I grew up mostly in a midwestern town, where my mom used to play conservative radio in the car. I don't recall listening to it much, it was just noise, but who knows? I could have taken it in. My dad stayed out of politics. We were an upper-middle class family that could afford to send me to a private school after grade school, and they did. I don't recall politics being a part of that education. In my own recollection, that education was fairly apolitical. I did have a history teacher who liked communism a lot, had a legit little red book and all, but all she did was push us to explore ideas. Maybe she was a communist, I don't really know, but it was really fascinating nonetheless. I also recall one incident where a freshman came into the senior lounge randomly, and we told him to leave. He then tried, I think, to race-bait us with "Is this because I'm black?" I said, "No, it's because you're a freshman, so leave." Maybe he didn't know it was the senior lounge. I don't know. He was also part of the NAACP club, which I only found out about because he won some NAACP award later in a ceremony.

In elementary school in the northeast, I remember our little class having a mock election (Dukakis vs. Reagan) and I think Dukakis won. I voted for Reagan, and I recall some other students sort of belittling me for it, but not that much - probably because I was not in the majority. We didn't know what we were voting for anyway, so what the hell.

Fast forward to college. Again, I recall it being fairly apolitical, but I was in a major that didn't lend itself well to political topics. The classes I did take outside of my major tended to lean left in terms of perspective, but it wasn't anything I found intolerable. Well, with the exception of freshman orientation where they invited a speaker where you had to admit you were racist So I used rational thinking and just signed in and left, because I figured nobody was actually taking attendance and I knew what the speaker was going to say before they said it. There were also sexual assault plays (those at least had some humor, so not that bad all in all). I think the plays came before the "I am a racist" speaker, so I figured the game out quick and stopped wasting my time. I already knew it's not okay to be racist and not okay to rape someone, thanks to my upbringing.

So after getting my undergrad degree, I meddled around in post-grad stuff, accumulated some more debt, transferred a few times, and ultimately never finished a post-grad.

I entered the work force, paid off my student debt, and haven't voted since college. I'm interested in politics to the extent that it was weird to me to see the stances of each party. From what I saw mostly growing up, both D and R liked the 1st amendment a lot, everyone agreed on that. The 2nd was an issue for D but was strongly supported by R. The other amendments hardly anyone talks or fights about. The R tended to take the stance of the religious right on cultural issues, and the D tended to take the not-stance of the religious right. I agreed more with D on the cultural issues, and the R on economic issues. I have never been a religious person, and probably never will be.
